title: Recurrent networks and LSTM, 1997
story:
A recurrent network reads a sequence one step at a time, carrying a hidden state forward from each step into the next. To learn that something early in the sequence explains something late in it, the error measured at the end has to travel back along that chain, through every step in between.

At each step it is multiplied. That is the whole difficulty, and it is arithmetic rather than engineering. Multiply a quantity by a factor smaller than one, fifty times over, and it is gone. Multiply it by a factor larger than one, fifty times over, and it is enormous. There is no third outcome unless the factor is one exactly, and nothing in a trained network arranges for that.

Hochreiter's 1991 diploma thesis identified the vanishing gradient problem formally: with standard activation functions the backpropagated error signal either shrinks rapidly or grows out of bounds, decaying exponentially in the number of steps it is carried back through. The same effect appears in deep feedforward networks and in recurrent ones, where it is called the long time lag problem. It is the same arithmetic in both, except that in a recurrent network the steps are moments in time rather than layers of a stack, so the depth is set by how long the sequence is rather than by anything you chose.

Then a stronger result, and the one worth sitting with. Bengio, Simard and Frasconi published Learning long-term dependencies with gradient descent is difficult in IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks in March 1994, showing that gradient-based learning faces an increasingly difficult problem as the duration of the dependency increases, and exposing a trade-off between efficient learning by gradient descent and latching information robustly for long periods: either the dynamics are not robust to noise, or the gradients vanish.

Read what kind of claim that is. It does not say the training was badly tuned or the network too small. It says the two properties you want are in conflict — the same stability that lets a unit hold a value against noise is what starves the gradient that would teach it. A trade-off cannot be tuned away, so the design has to change.

The change reads directly off the arithmetic. If the only factor that survives repetition is one exactly, then build a path through time whose factor is one exactly, by construction rather than by luck. Hochreiter and Schmidhuber published Long Short-Term Memory in Neural Computation in 1997, enforcing constant error flow through constant error carousels inside special units. Each carousel uses the identity function as its activation and a self-connection of fixed weight 1.0, so the derivative is constantly 1.0 and the error neither decays nor grows while it stays inside. The paper reports bridging minimal time lags in excess of 1000 discrete time steps, where previous recurrent networks failed at minimal lags of 10 steps.

Notice the shape of that solution, because it recurs everywhere. They did not find a better factor. They arranged for one path to do nothing at all. The carousel has no clever dynamics and computes nothing; its entire content is that it leaves the number alone, and the skill was knowing which number that had to be.

A path that leaves the number alone is not yet memory, because nothing decides what enters it or when it is read. That is what the multiplicative gate units are for: they learn to open and close access to the constant error flow. The gates are learned, the carousel is fixed, and the split is the design — the part that must not be disturbed is a constant, and the part that must adapt is the only part that adapts.

Now the piece the popular retelling drops, which is the piece this lesson turns on. Gers, Schmidhuber and Cummins published Learning to Forget: Continual Prediction with LSTM in Neural Computation in October 2000, identifying a weakness on continual input streams that are not segmented in advance into subsequences with explicitly marked ends at which the internal state could be reset. Without those resets the state may grow indefinitely and eventually cause the network to break down. Their remedy is an adaptive forget gate that enables a memory cell to learn to reset itself at appropriate times, releasing internal resources.

So the architecture built to stop a network forgetting was given, three years later, a learned mechanism for forgetting. That is not a retreat, and reading it as one misses the point. The requirement was never to never forget. It was to decide what to keep — and a store that nothing ever clears is not memory, it is a leak with a good reputation.

The failure is also a lesson in where the benchmark was doing work for you. Every algorithm they review, including the unmodified architecture, fails on continual versions of the benchmark problems, and with forget gates those same problems are solved easily. The architecture had not changed and the task had not become harder in any interesting sense. The segmented benchmarks had been supplying the reset for free, and nobody had to notice, because the end of each subsequence was marked in the data.

What remains true of all of it, and what eventually cost this design its place, is that the state is still computed one step after another. The carousel fixes what happens to the gradient along the chain. It does not remove the chain, and a computation that must walk a sequence in order cannot be spread across it.

problem.name: The long time lag problem
problem.shape: A signal has to survive a long chain of repeated steps, and every step multiplies it.
tell: the model must connect a cause to an effect many steps away
the depth is set by the length of the input rather than by the design
training improves on short examples and stalls on long ones
state accumulates on a stream with no marked end
a value must be held unchanged for a long time and also be learnable
problem.move: Stop looking for a better factor and build a path whose factor is one exactly, by construction: an identity unit with a fixed self-connection, so the error is unchanged along it. Keep every learned part off that path, and put learned gates around it to decide what enters, what is read, and when it is cleared.
problem.invariant: The error crossing the carousel is multiplied by a derivative of 1.0 at each step, so its magnitude does not depend on the length of the lag.
problem.breaks: The cell has no natural end. On a continual stream with no marked boundaries the state may grow indefinitely and eventually break the network down, which is why a learned reset had to be added in 2000 — and any benchmark that is segmented in advance hides this, because the data supplies the reset.

cost.time: the sequence is still walked one step after another, so the work along it cannot be spread out however the gradient is protected
cost.space: every cell carries state for the whole sequence, and gates multiply the parameters per unit
cost.beats: a plain recurrent network, which has the same expressive power on paper and cannot be trained across long lags, and a fixed-width window over the recent past, which is trainable but cannot see past its own edge

worked.problem: Why is depth in time harder than depth in layers, and what is a weight of one exactly protecting?
worked.reasoning:
Because depth in time is not a design choice, it is whatever the input is.

The mechanism is the same in both cases. An error signal travelling back through many steps is multiplied at every one of them, and a repeated factor smaller than one decays exponentially while a factor larger than one grows out of bounds. Hochreiter's 1991 diploma thesis identified this formally, and named the recurrent case the long time lag problem.

The difference is who chooses the number of steps. In a feedforward stack you do, and you can make it shallower, add connections that skip layers, or change the activation. In a recurrent network the sequence does, so the same network is shallow on a short input and hundreds of steps deep on a long one, and no architectural decision made in advance bounds it.

Bengio, Simard and Frasconi made this sharper in 1994 by showing a trade-off between efficient learning by gradient descent and latching information robustly for long periods: either the dynamics are not robust to noise, or the gradients vanish. That is the part I would emphasise, because it rules out the obvious answers. It is not a tuning problem. The stability that holds a value against noise is the same property that starves the gradient.

What a weight of one exactly is protecting is the only factor that survives repetition. Multiply by anything else enough times and you get zero or infinity, so the 1997 architecture builds a path whose factor is one by construction: the identity as the activation, a self-connection of fixed weight 1.0, a derivative that is constantly 1.0, and therefore an error that neither decays nor grows while it stays on that path. It reports bridging minimal time lags in excess of 1000 discrete time steps where previous recurrent networks failed at minimal lags of 10 steps.

The design insight worth stating is that the carousel computes nothing. Its whole job is to leave the number alone, and the learned parts are kept off it — the multiplicative gates open and close access to it, so the part that must not be disturbed is constant and the part that must adapt is separate.

And I would finish on the correction, because it shows what the requirement actually was. On continual streams that are not segmented in advance into subsequences with marked ends where the state could be reset, the state may grow indefinitely and break the network down, which is why the adaptive forget gate was added in 2000 to let a cell learn to reset itself. The design built to stop forgetting acquired a learned way to forget, and the earlier benchmarks had hidden the need only because their segmentation supplied the reset for free.

problem.practice: Take a recurrent network and train it to copy a symbol seen at the start of a sequence to the output at the end, then lengthen the gap: ten steps, fifty, two hundred. Find where it stops learning. The number itself does not matter; watching accuracy fall off a cliff as the only thing you changed was the distance is what makes the argument concrete.

beats.broke: An error travelling back across many steps is multiplied at every one, and a repeated factor other than one exactly either decays to nothing or grows out of bounds, so a cause far from its effect cannot be learned.
beats.fix: Build a path through time whose factor is one exactly — the identity as the activation and a self-connection of fixed weight 1.0 — and put learned multiplicative gates around it.
beats.cost: A cell nothing ever clears fills up on a stream with no marked ends, so a learned way to forget had to be added to the architecture built to stop forgetting.

interview.q: Why is depth in time harder than depth in layers, and what is a weight of one exactly protecting?
interview.trap: Describing the gates as the invention. The gates are the control surface; the invention is a path whose factor is one exactly, which is the only factor that survives repetition. Answering with the mechanism and not the arithmetic leaves you unable to say why any other design fails.
interview.answer:
Because depth in time is not a design choice — the input sets it, so the same network is shallow on a short sequence and hundreds of steps deep on a long one, and nothing decided in advance bounds it. In a feedforward stack you choose the depth and can make it shallower.

The mechanism is identical in both: an error going back through many steps is multiplied at each one, so a repeated factor below one decays exponentially and one above it grows out of bounds. Hochreiter's 1991 diploma thesis identified that formally, and in recurrent networks it is called the long time lag problem.

What rules out the obvious fixes is the 1994 result from Bengio, Simard and Frasconi: a trade-off between efficient learning by gradient descent and latching information robustly for long periods — either the dynamics are not robust to noise, or the gradients vanish. The stability that holds a value against noise is the same property that starves the gradient, so it is not a tuning problem.

A weight of one exactly is protecting the only factor that survives repetition. The 1997 architecture builds a path with that factor by construction: the identity as the activation, a self-connection of fixed weight 1.0, a derivative constantly 1.0, and so an error that neither decays nor grows while it stays on the path. It reports bridging minimal time lags in excess of 1000 discrete time steps where previous recurrent networks failed at minimal lags of 10 steps. The carousel computes nothing — its whole job is to leave the number alone — and the learned multiplicative gates are kept off it, opening and closing access to that error flow.

The correction is worth adding because it shows what the requirement really was. On continual streams that are not segmented in advance into subsequences with marked ends where the state could be reset, the state may grow indefinitely and break the network down, so an adaptive forget gate was added in 2000 to let a cell learn to reset itself. The design built to stop forgetting acquired a learned way to forget — the goal was never to never forget, it was to decide what to keep.
